blocks.x: Key definitions
Chart A visual representation of worksheet data used to reveal patterns, trends and comparisons that are harder to see in raw numbers. Charts are built using the Chart Wizard or the Insert tab.
Sorting Arranging data in a particular order — ascending (A–Z, smallest–largest) or descending (Z–A, largest–smallest) — based on the values in one or more columns.
Filtering Displaying only the rows of data that meet specified criteria, temporarily hiding rows that do not match, without deleting or rearranging any data.
Record vs. Field In a data table used for sorting/filtering, each row is a record (e.g. one student's full set of marks) and each column is a field (e.g. the CSM 201 mark for every student).
Chart Terminology & Types→ Creating & Saving Charts→ Sorting Data→ Filtering Data
The vocabulary of charts
Before building a chart, you need to know its parts and how Excel decides what goes on which axis — then pick from the 14 built-in chart types.
Why we use charts

A chart gives a visual summary of the patterns and trends hidden in a table of numbers — it is far easier to spot a rising trend, an outlier, or a proportion at a glance in a chart than by scanning rows of figures. Charts are created using the Chart Wizard or directly from the Insert tab, and once created they can live embedded in the same worksheet as the data, or on their own separate chart sheet. In either case, a chart built from worksheet cells is linked to that data — if the underlying numbers change, the chart automatically updates to reflect the new values.
What becomes the axis, and what becomes the legend

When you select a data range, Excel decides which dimension of your table becomes the category (x) axis and which becomes the legend labels. As a rule, Excel plots data so that the category axis runs along the longer side of the selected range (more rows than columns, or vice versa), while the labels along the shorter side become the legend entries or series names. Row/column headers included in the selection are used as text labels rather than plotted values.
Key chart terminology

Data Series
A set of related data points plotted in a chart, usually coming from one row or one column of the worksheet (e.g. all of one student's marks, or all students' CSM 201 marks). A chart can plot several data series at once.

Data Point
A single value from a data series, represented on the chart by one bar, one line segment, one pie slice, etc.

Legend
A key that identifies which color, pattern or marker corresponds to each data series on the chart.

Marker
The symbol (dot, square, triangle, etc.) used on a line or scatter chart to mark the position of an individual data point.
Axis A reference line along which data is measured or plotted — most 2-D charts have a horizontal category (x) axis and a vertical value (y) axis.

Tick mark
A small line of measurement that crosses an axis, dividing it into equal segments and lining up with the axis labels or gridlines.

Plot Area
The rectangular region bounded by the axes, inside which the data series themselves (bars, lines, slices) are actually drawn.

Chart Wizard button
A toolbar/ribbon control that walks you step-by-step through choosing a chart type, confirming the data range, adding titles/labels, and choosing where to place the finished chart.

Series formula
The formula bar entry (e.g. =SERIES(...)) that defines exactly which worksheet cells feed a given data series — this is what keeps the chart linked to its source data.

Toolbar
A row of buttons/icons (e.g. the Chart Tools ribbon) giving quick access to chart-formatting commands.

Tip (ScreenTip)
A small pop-up label that appears when the mouse hovers over a chart element, showing its name or exact value.
The 14 standard chart types

c: Column
Clustered (2-D/3-D), Stacked (2-D/3-D), 100% Stacked (2-D/3-D), Cylinder, Cone, Pyramid variants
Comparing values across categories using vertical bars; stacked forms show how parts make up a whole
Bar
Clustered, Stacked, 100% Stacked (2-D/3-D), Horizontal cylinder, cone, pyramid
Same comparisons as Column but horizontal — useful when category names are long
Line
Line with markers, Line / Line with markers, Stacked line, 100% stacked line, 3-D line
Showing trends over time (e.g. across months or years) with data plotted at even intervals
Pie
Pie / Pie in 3-D, Pie of pie, Bar of pie, Exploded pie / Exploded pie 3-D
Showing the proportion each part contributes to a single total (one data series only); "explode" pulls one slice out for emphasis
Doughnut
Doughnut, Exploded doughnut
Like a pie chart but can display more than one data series, each as a separate ring
Area
Area / Area 3-D, Stacked area, 100% stacked area, 3-D area
Emphasizing the magnitude of change over time by filling the area beneath each line
XY (Scatter)
Scatter with markers only, Scatter with smooth lines, Scatter with straight lines
Comparing pairs of numeric values when x-axis spacing is uneven, when there are many data points, or when comparing large datasets — not for evenly-spaced categories
Radar
Radar, Radar with markers, Filled radar
Comparing several data series across multiple variables/axes radiating from a center point
Surface
3-D Surface, Wireframe 3-D Surface, Contour, Wireframe Contour
Showing trends across two dimensions simultaneously using color bands/contours over a 3-D surface
Bubble
Bubble, Bubble with 3-D effect
Comparing three sets of values, where bubble size represents a third variable
Stock
High-Low-Close, Open-High-Low-Close, Volume-High-Low-Close, Volume-Open-High-Low-Close
Illustrating fluctuating values such as stock prices over time

blocks.title: Choosing between Pie, Doughnut and Bar of Pie

items: Pie: use when you have exactly one data series and want to show each category's share of one total (e.g. one term's grade distribution).
Doughnut: use when you need the same "share of a total" view but for more than one data series — each series becomes its own ring.
Pie of pie / Bar of pie: use when some slices are too small to read clearly — these subtypes pull the small slices into a secondary pie or bar for detail.
Exploded pie: right-click a slice and drag it outward (or set "point explosion") to separate and emphasize that one slice from the rest of the pie.

sections.title: Creating a chart step by step

blocks.x: From worksheet to picture
Two ways to build a chart — a guided manual route and a one-key automatic route — plus what happens to a chart when its source data changes.
Creating a chart step by step
Select data (incl. headers)→ Insert tab→ Choose chart type→ Choose format→ Add labels (Layout button)

items: 1Select the data you want charted, including the row/column headers — Excel uses these headers as axis labels and legend text.
2Go to the Insert tab on the ribbon and pick a chart category (Column, Line, Pie, etc.).
3Choose the specific chart type and format/subtype (e.g. Clustered Column 2-D) from the gallery that appears.
4Add or edit labels — chart title, axis titles, data labels, legend position — using the Layout button/tab that appears once the chart is inserted.

blocks.x: The F11 / Alt+F1 shortcut

F11 (or Alt+F1) With the data range selected, pressing F11 instantly creates a chart on a new chart sheet, while Alt+F1 instantly creates an embedded chart on the current worksheet. Both use Excel's default chart type, which out of the box is the 2-D Clustered Column chart.

items: The category axis is set to run along the longer side of the selected range (whichever of rows/columns has more entries).
Labels from the shorter side of the selection become the legend entries or the chart/series title.

If a column selected as "category" cells actually contains only numbers (not text), Excel may misread it as a data series in its own right rather than as labels, and will auto-number the categories (1, 2, 3, …) instead — so it is safer to include a text header row when selecting data for a chart.

blocks.x: What happens when the data changes

Because a chart is linked to its source cells through its series formula, it automatically updates whenever the values in that range change — edit a mark, and the corresponding bar or slice redraws itself. However, this automatic link only tracks the original range: if you later insert or delete rows/columns so the data range grows or shrinks, the chart may need to be manually redefined (by editing the chart's Select Data / series range) so the new or removed data is picked up correctly. A chart that has been printed or saved/pasted as a static image (e.g. copied as a picture) is no longer linked and will not update automatically.
Working with the finished chart

items: 1An embedded chart is simply an object on the worksheet, so it is saved automatically with the workbook — no separate save step is required.
2To print a chart, go to File > Print Preview, then use the Setup button to open Page Setup.
3On the Margins tab, you can adjust spacing around the chart, and the "Use Full Page" option scales the chart to fill the entire printed page.

sections.title: Sort A to Z / Sort Z to A

blocks.x: Putting rows in order
Sorting rearranges the records in a table into ascending or descending order, either by one field or by several fields with tie-breaking rules.

Sorting Arranging data in ascending (A→Z, smallest→largest, earliest→latest) or descending (Z→A, largest→smallest) order. In a data table, each row is treated as a record and each column as a field — sorting reorders whole records, keeping every field of a record together.
Sort A to Z / Sort Z to A

The quickest sort works on the first/leftmost column (or whichever cell is currently selected): click any cell in that column, then go to Home > Sort & Filter and choose Sort A to Z (ascending) or Sort Z to A (descending). Excel automatically extends the sort to the whole table, keeping each record's other fields aligned with it.
Custom Sort dialog

If you need to sort by a column that is not the first column, use Custom Sort instead of the one-click buttons: Home > Sort & Filter > Custom Sort opens the Sort dialog box, where you explicitly pick the column to sort by (from a dropdown, using the field/header names) and pick the order (A to Z / Z to A, or Smallest to Largest / Largest to Smallest).
Multi-column sort with a tiebreaker
A class list has columns Name, CSM 201 and CSM 203. Sort the table so students are ranked by CSM 201 mark ascending; for students who tie on CSM 201, break the tie using CSM 203 mark, highest first.

items: 1Select any cell inside the data table, then open the Sort dialog.Home > Sort & Filter > Custom Sort
2Set the primary sort level: column CSM 201, order Smallest to Largest (ascending).Sort by: CSM 201 — A to Z / Ascending
3Click "Add Level" to create a "Then By" rule for the tiebreaker.Add Level → new "Then By" row appears
4Set the secondary level: column CSM 203, order Largest to Smallest (descending), since ties are broken by the higher CSM 203 mark.Then by: CSM 203 — Z to A / Descending
5Click OK to apply the sort.Table re-orders: CSM 201 ascending, CSM 203 descending among ties

blocks.x: Result: rows are ordered by CSM 201 (low to high); any students sharing the same CSM 201 mark are then ordered by CSM 203 (high to low).

items: Each "Add Level" click adds one more "Then By" rule, applied only to break ties left by the level above it.
Levels can be reordered, removed, or set to different sort orders independently.
Sorting works on the whole record (row) at once — Name, CSM 201 and CSM 203 always move together, no matter which column drives the sort.

sections.title: Three ways to filter — used one at a time

blocks.x: Showing only what matters
Filtering hides the rows that don't meet a condition, without deleting or reordering any data — perfect for isolating students who need attention.

Filtering Displaying only the rows of a table that meet specified criteria, while temporarily hiding every row that does not match. Filtered-out rows are not deleted — they simply aren't shown until the filter is cleared.
Three ways to filter — used one at a time

items: 1By list values — tick the specific values you want to keep (e.g. only rows where the Programme is "Computer Science") from an auto-generated checklist.
2By format — show only rows whose cell has a particular fill color, font color, or icon (useful after conditional formatting).
3By criteria — show only rows meeting a logical/numeric condition, such as "less than," "greater than," or "between."

blocks.x: Important limitation You can filter by list values, by format, or by criteria — but Excel does not let you combine two of these methods on the same column at once (e.g. you cannot filter by both cell color and a value list simultaneously on one column).
Turning on AutoFilter
Select header row→ Sort & Filter > Filter→ Dropdown arrow on target column→ Number Filter > condition→ Enter threshold
Finding students who failed CSM 203
A class list has columns Name, CSM 201 and CSM 203, with the header row in row 1. Show only the students whose CSM 203 mark is below the pass mark of 40.

items: 1Select the header row of the table (Name, CSM 201, CSM 203) so Excel knows which row holds the field names.Select row 1
2Turn on filtering from the Home tab.Home > Sort & Filter > Filter
3Click the dropdown arrow that appears on the CSM 203 header.Click ▾ on "CSM 203"
4Choose the criteria-based filter for numbers, then the "Less Than" condition.Number Filters > Less Than…
5Enter the pass-mark threshold and confirm.Enter 40 > OK

blocks.x: Result: only rows where CSM 203 < 40 remain visible — every student who failed CSM 203 — while all other rows are temporarily hidden.

items: Greater Than — e.g. show only students who scored above 70 (distinction range).
Between — e.g. show only marks between 40 and 49 (borderline pass range).
Top 10 — show only the highest (or lowest) N values or percentage in a column.
Filters can be applied to more than one column at once, narrowing the visible rows to those meeting all active conditions together.
